content_html_sanitized:
Posted November 28, 2000
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Yesterday afternoon the DEAland Supreme Court agreed to give a fast track hearing on the federal government’s challenge to the 9th Circuit’s ruling that patients, who would suffer imminent harm from not using medical marijuana and have no reasonable alternative, have the right to buy – and hence the Oakland club has the right to sell -- medical marijuana.

Contrary to what has sometimes been reported, this is not a challenge to the various state medical marijuana laws. No such challenge has been mounted in any federal court, and the Supreme Court never goes beyond the narrow issues directly before it.
See
The Orange County Register Editorial Page Does the Best Job of Explaining the Significance of the Supreme Court’s Ruling on the Oakland Case.

Thus, an adverse ruling in this case would not strike down the state medical marijuana laws. In fact, this challenge is a very high-risk move for the Feds. They are challenging a very narrow medical necessity defense, one which exempts only those who face " imminent harm " and have " no reasonable alternative " to medical marijuana.

The Court agreed to hear the case last August, but it was not clear at the time whether they would hear it in this session of the court. Attorneys for the CBC opposed the fast track, believing that time is on our side. Also, the government has infinite resources to pour into the case, but at the same time the CBC’s lawyers recognized that there is an urgent need for a resolution.

The Court is expected to hear arguments on the Oakland case in April and rule in June.

The fact that the Court stayed the 9th Circuit ruling, thereby inflicting imminent harm on patients who have no reasonable alternative to medical marijuana, was seen as indicative of a negative bias. However, that is does not mean that they will necessarily uphold the government’s position.
See
Supreme Court Grants Emergency Stay Against Oakland CBC. Arbitrary Power Trumps Basic Rights.

In fact, the government’s argument that the drug war depends on inflicting harm on the sick and dying is rather pathetic. At the time, Justice John Paul Stevens, the lone dissenter in ordering the stay, said that the government " has failed to demonstrate that the denial of necessary medicine to seriously ill and dying patients will advance the public interest or that the failure to enjoin the distribution of such medicine will impair the orderly enforcement of federal criminal statutes.''

It is hard to imagine that he will be alone in the Court’s ultimate ruling, whether or not he is in the majority.

The government’s position is that marijuana has no medical value, simply because the Congress in its infinite wisdom has so voted. The government did not offer any evidence to support this contention. Had they offered such evidence, they would have opened themselves to having to argue on the merits. However, that does not stop the attorneys for the CBC from arguing the facts.

An adverse ruling by the Court will not stop the medical marijuana movement, but it would put the Justices in the position of saying that the ancient Anglo-Saxon Common Law right of " necessity " as a defense is less important than the arbitrary power of the government to prosecute the drug war.

That position took a direct hit in today’s ruling on Indianapolis " drug-check " roadblocks.

In a very important 6 to 3 ruling, the Court held that such stops violated the 4th Amendment’s protection against unreasonable searches:
" The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized. "

Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, who wrote the majority opinion, said the ruling does not affect other roadblocks, which the court has previously held to be constitutional, to detect drunken drivers and to intercept illegal immigrants being smuggled across the U.S. border by car. In the past, the court has suggested a roadblock to verify drivers' licenses and registrations would be permissible to serve a highway safety interest.

In the Indianapolis roadblocks, police did the usual things, checking licenses and vehicle registrations, looking for any signs of impairment, but they also had a drug-sniffing dog walk around the outside of each stopped car.

The city claimed that no one was stopped for more than five minutes. In six roadblocks between August and November 1998, more than 1,100 vehicles were stopped and 104 people were arrested -- half for drug offenses and half on other charges. This means that more than 90% of the stops yielded no arrests.

O'Connor said the court has never approved a checkpoint program whose primary purpose was to detect evidence of ordinary criminal wrongdoing. If just looking for drugs was sufficient reason, the police could use roadblocks for almost any conceivable purpose, she said.

Perhaps the most important part of the ruling was the rejection of the " drug problem " as a general justification for anything and everything, as has often been the case in the past. This bodes well for future rulings, especially on medical necessity.

On the other hand, the court's most conservative members, Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justices Clarence Thomas and Antonin Scalia, dissented. Oddly, these men consider themselves " strict constructionists " -- who defend the original intent of the framers. It is hard to imagine how Madison and Jefferson would tolerate the drug war.

Rehnquist wrote, " These stops effectively serve the state's legitimate interests; they are executed in a regularized and neutral manner; and they only minimally intrude upon the privacy of motorists.'' He said the Indianapolis program were consistent with other rulings allowing roadblocks for traffic safety-- and the addition of a dog sniffing around the car did not add to the length or intrusion of the stop.

Will they argue that patients who will suffer imminent harm because they have no reasonable alternative to medical marijuana would suffer only minimal intrusion on their rights? It would seem to me to be a much more difficult argument for the government’s lawyers. The Indianapolis ruling gives reason for hope.

Perhaps the Supreme Court really does follow the election returns.
